1.5× / 1.55× ANAMORPHIC GUIDE

How to Desqueeze 1.5x Anamorphic Video

1.5× and 1.55× footage gives a stronger widescreen look than 1.33×. Use the correct horizontal correction to restore natural geometry without making faces or objects look too wide.

1.5× WORKFLOW

Correct stronger anamorphic footage with confidence.

STEP 1

Confirm the squeeze

Check whether the footage was shot with a 1.5× or 1.55× anamorphic lens or preset.

STEP 2

Test both values

Compare 1.5× and 1.55× when the exact lens value is unclear.

STEP 3

Watch faces and circles

Stronger factors can over-stretch quickly, so check natural geometry before export.

STEP 4

Deliver wider frames

Use the corrected image for cinematic widescreen, edit handoff, or final app export.

WHAT 1.5× DOES

1.5× expands the frame more than 1.33×.

Stronger squeeze

More width stored in-frame

1.5× footage stores more horizontal field of view inside the recorded frame.

1.5× / 1.55× correction

More horizontal stretch than 1.33×

The preview stretches width more aggressively than 1.33× while keeping height unchanged.

Wider delivery

Cinematic, still natural

After correction, the frame can feel more cinematic, but must still preserve natural faces and shapes.

WHEN TO USE 1.5×

Use 1.5× or 1.55× when 1.33× is not enough.

1.33× still looks squeezed

If 1.33× correction still looks tall or narrow, test 1.5× next.

Lens says 1.5×

If the lens or preset states 1.5×, use that value first.

Lens says 1.55×

Some adapters and presets use 1.55×. Compare with 1.5× if unsure.

Faces must stay natural

If faces look too wide, the correction is probably too strong.

Better for wider looks

1.5× / 1.55× can create a more dramatic widescreen feel than 1.33×.

Quick check: compare 1.5× and 1.55× using faces, wheels, lights, and straight vertical lines. Choose the value that looks natural, not just the widest.

COMPARE RATIOS

1.5× sits between mobile 1.33× and classic 2×.

1.33×

Lighter correction, common for mobile anamorphic footage and fast social workflows.

1.5× / 1.55×

Stronger correction with a wider cinematic look while still being manageable for mobile or compact workflows.

2.0×

Heavier correction used for classic cinema-style anamorphic footage and very wide framing.

Light-squeeze workflows: 1.33× guide · Browser preview: Desqueeze online

1.5× MISTAKES

Common 1.5× / 1.55× desqueeze mistakes.

Treating 1.5× like 1.33×

A 1.5× lens needs stronger correction. 1.33× may still look squeezed.

Over-correcting to 2×

2× can make 1.5× footage look unnaturally wide.

Ignoring 1.55× presets

If your lens or app uses 1.55×, compare it against 1.5× before final export.

Choosing the widest look

The correct factor is the one that restores natural geometry, not always the widest image.

Checking only landscapes

Landscapes can hide distortion. Use faces, circles, and objects with known shapes.

Exporting before comparison

Preview 1.5× and 1.55× side by side before committing to final output.

FAQ

1.5× / 1.55× quick answers

Should I use 1.5× or 1.55×?
Use the lens or app preset value first. If unsure, compare both and choose the one where faces and circles look natural.
Is 1.5× more cinematic than 1.33×?
It creates a stronger widescreen look, but the correct choice depends on the lens used during capture.
What happens if I use 2× on 1.5× footage?
The image will usually look over-stretched, with faces and circular objects becoming too wide.
Can I use 1.5× for mobile footage?
Yes, if the footage was captured with a 1.5× or 1.55× lens or preset. Do not use it just to make footage wider.
